title: Russell on his Monza prospects after loss to ‘flying’ Gasly
excerpt:
George Russell shared his predictions for the Italian Grand Prix after settling for second place in Qualifying, as Alpine driver Pierre Gasly executed a remarkable lap to clinch pole position at the last moment.

With the second Mercedes of Kimi Antonelli set to start at the back of the grid, and Ferrari struggling to replicate their timesheet-topping pace from earlier in the weekend, it looked as though Russell had a relatively clear path to pole position.

His first effort – assisted by a tow from his team mate – saw him take P1 early in Q3, and while he complained about “front locking and instability” in the car, Russell went even faster on his final lap.

However, the possibility of a shock result quickly grew as Gasly also improved after showing eye-catching speed through the session, and the Frenchman ultimately snatched pole by a margin of 0.060s.

“Firstly, massive congrats to Pierre because that's an incredible performance,” Russell reflected. “We were actually finishing a game of chess about 15 minutes before Qualifying and he beat me there, but I thought 'well I'll beat you on Qualifying' and here we are!

“He's ahead of me again, so huge congrats to him. Of course I was disappointed not to get the pole position, was a bit messy with [Max] Verstappen opening the lap.

“I did the lap very close but Pierre and Alpine have been super fast, even from Q1, so happy to see them get a good result.”

He will be hoping to capitalise on both his front-row start and Antonelli’s grid penalty to recover some points in the Drivers’ Championship, where he sits in second place 59 points adrift of the Italian.

Despite the unlikely way Qualifying unfolded, he maintained that it didn’t impact his optimism for the rest of the weekend due to the numerous overtaking spots that Monza offers.

“Of all the circuits, this is probably the least important one to be on pole for [to] fight for victory,” Russell explained. “I was very happy to see Pierre on pole because he’s a great driver, a great person, hasn't had many opportunities of having the car beneath him to fight for pole. This weekend they were flying.

“We’re going to probably look back on the data from FP2 a bit more closely now because we didn’t really think they were a threat at all.

“We knew they looked more competitive, but sometimes teams are running less fuel or they’re using high power in practice. I wouldn’t say we disregarded it, but I don’t think anybody expected them to be fighting for pole.”

title: Ferrari drivers critical of Italy Qualifying strategy
excerpt:
Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton admit that Ferrari failed to execute a good enough strategy during Qualifying for the Italian Grand Prix, with the pair only achieving P4 and P5 respectively.

With the slipstream at Monza proving pivotal, teams and drivers tried to work in unison to give themselves a shot at pole position ahead of Sunday's 53-lap race.

But the Scuderia failed to deliver in front of their home fans, as both Leclerc and Hamilton found themselves two tenths adrift of surprise polesitter, Pierre Gasly.

The pair had been fortunate to even reach the final stage of Qualifying, as both were left on the cusp of Q2 elimination, with Hamilton only squeezing through by 0.001s over Gabriel Bortoleto's Audi.

"A very tough session, just in terms of getting consistency and ultimately we didn't do it, I think. Didn't execute that well," said Hamilton.

"My first lap felt really good in Q1 and I stopped to save the tyre, and then went into Q2 and I was meant to do a push-cool-cool-push.

"But because Charles didn't want to go out, they just delayed, delayed, so I only got one push and yeah, that was basically the whole session."

Leclerc admitted that the session had been messy in general, as well as having a technical issue which put himself and the team on the back foot.

"We've had way too many problems. Unfortunately, Q2 we had a big problem with the battery which then we understood, we kind of fixed for Q3, but just a messy session," he said.

"When you want to go and get the last hundredths, we need to be perfect as a team and we haven't been, so we need look at what's going on."

Leclerc was keen to stress that the result might have been different had Ferrari executed better, something he believed Gasly and Alpine achieved with a shock result.

"I spoke to Pierre yesterday and he was asking me some things for Turns 6-7. I was like, okay, with Pierre I can share things – and today he beat all of us for pole," added Leclerc.

"I'm very happy for Pierre. I think it's a big, big surprise for everybody, but it shows that with these cars, especially on tracks like this, if you do everything perfect then it can make a massive difference.

"I don't think they've got the best car, but I think they have done the best job today and, on a track like this, it makes a much bigger difference to other tracks."

One solace that the Ferrari pair can take after their struggles in Qualifying, is after Oscar Piastri's three-place grid penalty for impeding Liam Lawson in the first turn, it'll be an all-red second row as Leclerc and Hamilton have been pushed up to third and fourth respectively.

title: Duerksen wins F2 Monza Sprint Race from seventh
excerpt:
Joshua Duerksen claimed his third Sprint Race victory of the 2026 FIA Formula 2 season, fighting through the pack in impressive fashion to take the win.

The Invicta Racing driver started seventh on the grid, but was up to fourth place almost immediately by the time the pack reached Turn 4 on the opening lap.

From there, the Paraguayan driver picked off his rivals to climb the podium rankings, before a mid-race Safety Car wiped out reverse grid polesitter John Bennett’s lead.

At the restart, Duerksen stuck with the TRIDENT driver and eventually claimed the lead of the race with a straightforward DRS pass.

There was one more task to overcome however with a late Safety Car restart just a handful of laps remaining. Duerksen got a great restart and handled things from there, allowing the Mercedes Development Driver to take his third win of the campaign.

Bennett was second in the end, sticking with but unable to re-pass the winner in the closing laps, while MP Motorsport’s Oliver Goethe completed the podium in P3.

In the title fight, Nikola Tsolov earned points in fifth position, with Alexander Dunne keeping his hopes alive in seventh.

Second and third in the championship, Gabriele Mini and Rafael Camara, failed to score, with the former ending up P10, while Camara was a mid-race retirement after contact left him facing backwards and out of the race.

title: Alpine targeting Monza win after Gasly pole
excerpt:
Alpine Managing Director Steve Nielsen has set out the team’s ambition to “try and win it” at the Italian Grand Prix after Pierre Gasly claimed an impressive pole position for the Enstone-based squad.

Having displayed strong pace throughout Qualifying – which saw him lead the timesheets in Q1 – Gasly managed to go fastest of all during the final segment to score his maiden pole in Formula 1, six years on from his debut victory at the same circuit.

Speaking to Sky Sports F1 following the session, Nielsen praised the team for handling the busy track conditions well and successfully carrying out tows for Gasly and team mate Franco Colapinto.

“We put a big upgrade on Pierre's car in Zandvoort. That's also on Franco's car here,” said Nielsen. “I don't think we quite got the best out of the package in Zandvoort – it's a bit of a quirky circuit, but we've come here and the car is responding very well.

“We got the gaps right, we got the tows right. The drivers didn't make a mistake, and the lap time's clearly in the car, because both cars were quite quick.

“[The difference of a tow is] pretty big. A couple of tenths either way here is the difference between several places. If you get the tow, it's important.”

Nielsen went on to praise the performance of Gasly, hailing the 30-year-old as a “class act”.

“If you give him the machine, he'll deliver,” the Briton said. “We failed to do that a few times last year, and we haven't always given him the most competitive machinery this year, but when we have, he's delivered, particularly earlier in the season.

“So to see the team bounce back, to see him deliver on a track he knows well – he lives locally, he lives in Milan – it's wonderful. And of course, we mustn't forget Franco either. He did a great job today, so I really feel we've given them a good car, and who knows, anything's possible tomorrow.”

In terms of the prospects for race day, Nielsen suggested that the team’s “not very draggy” package should prove beneficial in that they could be “difficult to pass”.

“We didn't expect to be on pole position,“ he conceded. “We are. Tomorrow, [if we get] good starts, good strategy, good pit stops – who knows? Let's try and win it.”

title: Piastri hit with three-place grid penalty at Monza
excerpt:
Oscar Piastri has been handed a three-place grid penalty for the Italian Grand Prix after the stewards found him guilty of impeding Liam Lawson in Qualifying.

Red Bull substitute Lawson closed in on Piastri’s McLaren (which had just left the pits) through Monza’s first chicane during the closing stages of Q2 – the New Zealander subsequently expressing his frustration over the radio and missing the Q3 cut.

After hearing from both drivers, Red Bull and McLaren team representatives, and reviewing the range of data available to them, the stewarding panel settled on a grid drop for the Australian.

That means Piastri will fall from third to sixth on the grid, promoting Ferrari pair Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton, as well as the Red Bull of Lawson’s team mate, Max Verstappen.

Lawson meanwhile, is set to start from the back of the grid due to his Red Bull being fitted with new power unit components.

The stewards’ decision document and explanation read: “On leaving the pits, the driver of Car 81 (Piastri) was advised that ‘Verstappen, Lawson and Sainz just crossing, Sainz has pitted, just Verstappen and Lawson, watch out for them as you join’.

“The driver of Car 81 stated that he was not alerted to the fact that VER and LAW were on push laps, but realised as he was almost at Turn 1 that VER was on a push lap. He slowed significantly and kept to the right to allow VER to pass, but was unable to do anything to avoid impeding LAW who was close behind.

“The stewards accept that with the information he had, and the situation he was placed in, the driver of Car 81 had, at this stage, no other options available and hence, inadvertently, and also unnecessarily, impeded Car 30.”

Giving his take before the penalty was applied, Piastri said: “It was a tricky situation to manage. I was coming out of the pits and got told that Lawson and Verstappen were coming, but I kind of had to jump on the brakes pretty heavily to get out of Max’s way, and then I was just stuck in a very awkward spot with Liam.”

Lawson, meanwhile, said: “To be honest, we should really have the speed to get through [to Q3] anyway. We had quite good speed yesterday, and then today, we’ve lost some performance.

“In general, the goal was to obviously try and help Max in Q3 and I never got there, so it’s not what we planned for, but I think our Qualifying was a bit compromised anyway.”

title: Gasly reacts to shock pole position for Italian GP
excerpt:
Pierre Gasly was suitably delighted after the Alpine driver caused an upset to claim pole position for the first time in his F1 career during Saturday’s Qualifying session at the Autodromo Nazionale Monza.

Having impressed throughout the Q1 and Q2 phases, Gasly posted a stunning time of 1m 21.786s on his final Q3 run to jump ahead of Mercedes’ George Russell and McLaren’s Oscar Piastri.

That earned the Frenchman a maiden pole to go with the breakthrough victory he achieved around the Temple of Speed with the then-named AlphaTauri team (now Racing Bulls) back in 2020.

Speaking after he jumped out of the car and embraced Alpine team members, Gasly beamed: “It was amazing. It was an incredible Qualifying.

“From the first lap in Q1, I felt very good in the car. I was trying to chip a little bit away every single session and then in the end [in Q3], it felt like a very good lap.

“I’m so happy. It’s been nine years [in F1] trying to chase and get the opportunity to take pole position. I won my first race in Monza, and to get my first pole position on this track… I think is something special around here.”

Asked in his subsequent F1 TV interview where that result came from, Gasly laughed: “I’d like to tell you, but I don’t know! I’m so happy. I’m so pleased for all the guys, for the whole team, for myself.

“To feel these emotions, seeing on the last lap… putting everything out there and being rewarded for it, it’s just very special.

“I’m very grateful for the race car I’ve had today. I felt very confident, very comfortable to absolutely put everything there was out there, and squeeze every hundredth out of it on the last lap. I’m going to enjoy that one!”

Gasly admitted to feeling continuously surprised by his and Alpine’s progression throughout the weekend – which began with him missing FP1 to give reserve driver Paul Aron another run out.

“I didn’t drive in P1, which is never too great, then P2 was not ideal,” he said. “I felt like there was potential in the car, and in P3 I felt again better. I never really had a tow the whole Free Practice.

“Quali already Q1 I was P1, and I was a little surprised, ‘Okay, others are going to turn it up’. Q2 we were still up there, and Q3 run one, I found myself in P3. I was like, ‘I’ve never thought about it, but actually today I might get a shot at it!’”

Alpine’s day was made even better by the recently re-signed Franco Colapinto also making it into Q3 and placing eighth, which will become seventh when Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli takes a grid penalty for a power unit change.

Colapinto took his hat off to Gasly post-session, describing the result as “amazing” for Alpine as they recover from a mid-season slump.

“Q1 I was in the same lap time [as Gasly], and then he kept doing big steps, and my steps were smaller,” explained Colapinto. “Personally, I need to understand and learn from that, how he improved so much session after session, and he was doing big steps.

“I’m happy for the team. It’s an impressive result for the team. It’s amazing to do it here in Monza. Seeing both cars in Q3 is very positive, but even more when one is on pole.”

title: Verstappen rues Red Bull 'problem' in Italy Qualifying
excerpt:
Max Verstappen has confirmed that he "immediately picked up a problem" at the start of Qualifying for the Italian Grand Prix that limited the Red Bull driver to only fifth on the grid.

The four-time World Champion was less than three tenths behind surprise polesitter Pierre Gasly ahead of Sunday's 53-lap race at Monza, and also had no tow from a car in front on his final effort in Q3.

The Dutchman had complained about a "broken" rear axle earlier in proceedings, admitting after Qualifying that it had limited what was possible.

"I think FP3 was actually quite decent for us. We made a really good step overnight, but unfortunately going into Qualifying on my first lap I immediately picked up a problem on the rear axle, which we have already a lot during the season," said Verstappen.

"It happens at different phases on the weekend, unfortunately it happened in Qualifying so you just jump around a lot more, the car is not good on the kerbs anymore, the bumps, and it's just costing performance on a track where it is of course super close."

When asked if he could challenge for a podium, Verstappen added: "If we can fix it then yes, I think the car will be in a better window.

"Is that enough for a podium? I don't know. We'd like to race with a car that is 100%, that would be nice."

Red Bull team mate Liam Lawson, still standing in for the injured Isack Hadjar, failed to reach Q3 after only setting the 13th quickest time, with the New Zealander set to start at the back of the grid after power unit changes.

Knowing that he would not feature in the main battle for pole, much of Lawson's focus was on long runs and he only received a tow from Verstappen for his final Q2 effort.

But being blocked at the first chicane by McLaren's Oscar Piastri, with the Australian handed a grid penalty, prevented Lawson from advancing and ultimately helping Verstappen.

"We had quite good speed yesterday and then today, we've lost some performance. In general, the goal was to obviously try and help Max in Q3 and I never got there, so it's not what we planned for, but I think our Qualifying was a bit compromised anyway," he said.

"The weekend in general has just been focused on the race anyway because we knew we were taking the penalty.

"It's not ideal, we didn't put that much focus on just the pure one-lap speed, but outside of that, obviously getting blocked in Turn 1 doesn't help.

"I spent the whole of Qualifying in clean air until that last lap as well, so I hadn't even driven behind a car before. Wasn't ideal."

title: Lawson to start from the back at Monza after engine penalty
excerpt:
Liam Lawson has become the latest driver set to start from the back of the grid at the Italian Grand Prix due to his Red Bull being fitted with new power unit components.

A document released by the FIA confirms that the RB22 has taken on several new parts, including a sixth internal combustion engine, turbocharger and exhaust set, as well as its fourth MGU-K and seventh PU-ANC.

With these all exceeding the allocated number for each, Lawson will receive a grid penalty – meaning that he joins Mercedes’ Kimi Antonelli and Williams’ Alex Albon in starting from the back.

The allocation refers to parts used for the Red Bull usually driven by Isack Hadjar, with Lawson continuing to substitute while the Frenchman continues his rehabilitation from a wrist injury.

Yuki Tsunoda, meanwhile, is again sitting in for Lawson at Racing Bulls.

It marks the second consecutive outing in the RB22 for Lawson, who claimed points with a P7 finish last time out in Zandvoort.

title: Gasly charges to maiden F1 pole at Monza over Russell and Piastri
excerpt:
Alpine driver Pierre Gasly earned a brilliant first-ever F1 pole position at the Italian Grand Prix, edging out Mercedes’ George Russell and McLaren’s Oscar Piastri in a pulsating Qualifying session around the Autodromo Nazionale Monza.

Gasly, who claimed his maiden F1 win at the Temple of Speed back in 2020, featured towards the front of the times throughout Saturday’s Qualifying hour, as the Frenchman and his recently updated, Mercedes-powered car shone.

Sitting third to Russell and Piastri after the opening Q3 runs, Gasly sent shockwaves through the paddock when he pumped in a time of 1m 21.786s on his final lap – launching ahead of his Mercedes and McLaren rivals in the process.

Behind them, Ferrari’s practice form faded and resulted in P4 and P5 for Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton, with Max Verstappen sixth for Red Bull and home racer Kimi Antonelli seventh in the other Silver Arrow, prior to taking his engine penalty.

Franco Colapinto made it two cars in the final phase for Alpine, as the re-signed Argentinian placed eighth, ahead of Lando Norris (who, like team mate Piastri, struggled with his brakes throughout Qualifying) and Racing Bulls’ Arvid Lindblad.

Hamilton’s place in Q3 was secured by the finest of margins, with Audi’s Gabriel Bortoleto only one thousandth of a second slower across their final Q2 runs, leaving the Brazilian 11th on the grid from Ollie Bearman’s upgraded Haas-Ferrari and team mate Nico Hulkenberg.

Liam Lawson, also taking a grid drop for a power unit change this weekend, ended Qualifying down in 14th position, having been impeded by Piastri on his final Q2 lap, in an incident the stewards noted.

After his encouraging performance at the Dutch Grand Prix last time out, Yuki Tsunoda’s second weekend as a Racing Bulls stand-in is proving to be more challenging – the Japanese racer falling at the first Qualifying hurdle in 17th, while Lindblad placed fifth.

Another driver with an engine-related grid penalty, Alexander Albon played the team game by giving a Q1 tow to Sainz, putting the Briton 18th, ahead of only Cadillac drivers Valtteri Bottas and Sergio Perez, and the Aston Martins of Fernando Alonso and Lance Stroll.

AS IT HAPPENED

Q1 – Gasly impresses as tow games begin

After Saturday’s third and final practice session, topped by Russell over Hamilton and Verstappen, attention swiftly turned to Qualifying, and how the battle for pole position – gaining an effective tow again looking set to be a key part of that – would play out.

When the green light switched on at the end of the pit lane at 1600 local time and Q1 began, three drivers knew they would be dropping down the grid as a result of power unit changes and penalties – those being championship leader Antonelli, Albon and Lawson.

It begged an obvious question: would Antonelli and Lawson be used to assist Russell and Verstappen’s respective Q3 bids? First, they all had to get there, with the field squabbling for track position – and that fine balance between clear air and a slipstream – in the early stages of the opening phase.

While the Mercedes, Racing Bulls and Alpine cars bided their time in the pits, the first flurry of lap times brought a 1m 22.631s from Verstappen, followed closely by Hamilton, Piastri, and Leclerc, with Norris backing out of a lap but going again and slotting into fifth.

A few minutes later, Gasly (1m 22.612s) and Colapinto (1m 22.662s) surged to P1 and P3, sandwiching Verstappen’s Red Bull, before Antonelli took P4 and Russell P5 (the latter on mediums, rather than softs) with efforts in the 1m 22.7s bracket.

Another eye-catching lap then came from Bearman with his upgraded Haas machine and new Ferrari power unit, which put him a provisional P8, between the works red cars of Hamilton and Leclerc, and the papaya McLarens of Piastri and Norris.

At the other end of the timing screen, Hulkenberg, Albon, Bottas, Alonso, Stroll and Perez were the drivers in the drop zone, with some five minutes left on the Q1 clock and another round of laps set to follow through to the chequered flag.

After the slipstreaming train of cars had crossed the line one more time, Gasly was confirmed as the Q1 pace-setter with his earlier effort, in front of Verstappen, an improved Norris, Colapinto and FP3 star Lindblad, who also made gains on his final run.

All was not well at McLaren, though, with Norris asking his engineer, “Is there nothing else I can do about these brakes right now? I just think it’s going to go wrong into Turn 1.” His team mate, Piastri, had similar struggles en route to P11, behind the Mercedes and Ferrari cars, and Bearman’s Haas.

Bortoleto and Hulkenberg made it safely through to Q2 for Audi in P12 and P14, around the other Red Bull of Lawson, with Sainz (aided by a tow from his team mate) and Ocon the final drivers to progress at the expense of a struggling Tsunoda, Albon, the Cadillacs and the Aston Martins.

Knocked out: Tsunoda, Albon, Bottas, Perez, Alonso, Stroll

Q2 – Antonelli fastest as Hamilton squeezes through

After a short break, Q2 got under way, with Red Bull quick to make their move and deliver banker laps – Verstappen clocking a 1m 22.573s and Lawson a 1m 22.828s. All was not well for the Dutchman, as he reported: “The car is broken on the rear axle again. It’s really undriveable in Turn 2, 4 and 5.”

Once the rest of the remaining 16 drivers had got in on the action, Piastri held the P1 time on a 1m 22.017s, just ahead of team mate Norris, with Gasly again flying high in third from Mercedes pair Russell and Antonelli, Lindblad, Colapinto and Leclerc.

Hamilton, meanwhile, was back in 11th, behind Bortoleto and Verstappen, meaning the seven-time World Champion had work to do on his second run. Bearman, Lawson, Hulkenberg, Sainz and Ocon were the other drivers in the drop zone at this point.

Amid a flurry of improvements, Antonelli finished Q2 at the top of the times via a 1m 21.882s, from the McLarens, Gasly’s Alpine, team mate Russell and Verstappen, with Lindblad, Colapinto, Leclerc and an under-pressure Hamilton grabbing the final Q3 spots.

It was a genuine scare for Hamilton, who wound up just 0.001s faster than Bortoleto, while there were no other significant changes in the drop zone – Lawson left furious at being baulked by Piastri through the first chicane, which the stewards duly noted.

Knocked out: Bortoleto, Bearman, Hulkenberg, Lawson, Sainz, Ocon

Q3 – Gasly shocks rivals for maiden F1 pole

Another breather behind them, the top-10 drivers emerged from the pits for the decisive pole position shoot-out – Russell getting a tow from Antonelli en route to a provisional P1 time of 1m 21.929s, marginally up on Piastri and Gasly.

Leclerc was the fastest Ferrari driver over the first runs in fourth, ahead of Verstappen, Norris, Lindblad, team mate Hamilton and Colapinto. Antonelli then completed a lap out of sync with his rivals – after that tow for Russell – to move up to sixth place.

Despite sitting at the top of the order, Russell was not feeling comfortable behind the wheel of his Mercedes. “I’m really struggling with the car compared to FP3,” he commented over the radio. “Just front locking and instability in high-speed.”

Drama ensued at the start of the final runs when Piastri again missed his entry to the first chicane, but there were plenty of green and purple sector times behind – particularly from Gasly and his Alpine.

As the mini-sectors ticked by, an upset looked more and more possible, with Gasly ultimately posting a 1m21.786s to jump ahead of Piastri and Russell (despite the latter’s own improvement) and take pole for the first time in F1.

While Gasly screamed over the radio in delight, the Ferraris of Leclerc and Hamilton had to settle for fourth and fifth, as Verstappen, Antonelli (before his penalty), Colapinto, Norris (who failed to improve on his last lap) and Lindblad completed the Q3 order.

Key quote

“It was amazing,” said Gasly afterwards. “It was an incredible Qualifying. From the first lap in Q1, I felt very good in the car. I was trying to chip a little bit away every single session and then in the end [in Q3], it felt like a very good lap. I’m so happy. It’s been nine years trying to chase and get the opportunity to take pole position. I won my first race in Monza, and to get my first pole position on this track… I think is something special around here.”

title: ‘Who am I without racing?’ – Fewtrell on work with Quadrant
excerpt:
For every driver who reaches Formula 1, there are countless others whose journey through the junior ranks ends somewhere along the way. For those who have spent almost their entire lives racing, stepping away can mean figuring out not only what comes next, but who they are without it.

Throughout much of Max Fewtrell’s childhood, life followed the rhythm of a racing calendar. There was always another weekend to prepare for, another result to chase and, ultimately, one destination in mind – Formula 1.

These days, Fewtrell remains part of the F1 world through Quadrant. Ahead of the Italian Grand Prix, he'll join fans at F1 Arcade in London for a live race watch-along, but his motorsport journey once pointed in a very different direction.

Fewtrell became a British F4 champion before winning the Formula Renault Eurocup, competing against some of the young drivers who would eventually make it onto the F1 grid.

But his own path came to an end during the 2020 Formula 3 season – except, for Fewtrell, it did not initially feel like an ending at all.

“We spoke to teams here and there, slowly realising doors were closing for the next season,” Fewtrell tells F1.com in an exclusive chat. “We were looking at it like, ‘Okay, this whole year might be a write-off, but we'll try to do some testing and get a team in for F2 the year after.’ But as time went on, that wasn't looking realistic with the lack of sponsors.

“There wasn't even a defining day where I thought, ‘Oh, I'm never going to race again.’ It just sort of didn't happen again.”

Adjusting to life away from the track

For someone who had been racing since the age of nine, losing the rhythm of race weekends meant losing much of the structure around which his life had been built. As the months turned into years, Fewtrell found himself confronting a difficult question: who was he without racing?

“I'm still sort of figuring that out now,” he admits. “Not having a race weekend to look forward to or train for was really strange because I'd done that since I was nine years old. It was a massive change.”

What initially felt like a temporary pause gradually became something more permanent, forcing Fewtrell to reassess his future. “As it went on longer, it became more difficult to deal with and cope,” he says. “That's when I really started to question, ‘Who am I without racing? What am I going to do?’”

Six years on from stepping away midway through a Formula 3 season, Fewtrell can look back on the decision with more perspective, though not without some lingering doubts. “I'm 50-50 with the decision now,” he reflects. “Maybe I should have stuck the season out, stayed around it and been in people's vision. You never know what doors that can open eventually. It's always easy in hindsight.”

While gaming, golf and padel continue to satisfy his competitive instincts, Fewtrell admits nothing can replicate the emotions he experienced behind the wheel. “Nothing replicates that feeling of a good result. I've never felt the butterflies I had when I was sat on the grid. I don't know how I'll ever replicate that. That's something I struggle with. I miss it massively.”

2025 F1 World Champion Lando Norris' co-founds new junior single-seater team

Watching Norris become World Champion

There is another unusual element to Fewtrell's life after racing – his best friend is reigning World Champion Lando Norris.

Fewtrell and Norris were friends long before Formula 1 success. They were team mates in karting and followed similar junior paths, both winning British F4 and Formula Renault Eurocup titles before their careers diverged.

Fewtrell has remained close enough to see the reality of Formula 1 first-hand, travelling to races and watching Norris compete. Unsurprisingly, it has occasionally made him consider the path his own career might have taken.

“There's never any jealousy,” he says. “I've always been super proud, and it’s been amazing seeing him perform the way he does.

“There's always that ‘what if I made it?’, and you can see how his life has changed. I can see it first-hand. It’s the dream.

“But it's been cool to be close to that world of F1 and see it through a driver's eyes in a way. Being very close to him, I get to see what it's like to be a driver. I don't ever wonder... I know what it's like now. I've seen it through him.”

That perspective became particularly poignant in 2025, when Norris achieved the goal they had both once chased and became Formula 1 World Champion for the first time.

“I think he took such a big step mentally to overcome that hurdle,” Fewtrell says. “I don't know what that pressure would be like because I never made it there, so to see him do that has been amazing.”

Yet Fewtrell says the person he grew up alongside remains the same.

“I've not seen a massive change in him personally,” he explains. “Obviously, we've all matured from when we were 13 to now when we're 27. We're very different people, but I think the Lando inside is definitely the same.

"He’s very generous, very kind. A lot of people maybe don't see the full side of him, which is fine. He keeps it private, but he's definitely the same person that I grew up with, still the same guy.”

How Fewtrell became Quadrant’s Managing Partner

When Lando Norris launched Quadrant in 2020, Fewtrell got involved simply as a friend. No longer racing and still hoping to return to the grid, he joined Norris in making content.

“First of all, I was bored!” Fewtrell laughs. “I wasn't racing, so I had nothing to do. It looked fun, and he was like, ‘Look, I'd like to have a friend come and do this with me’, because he was on his own doing that.

“He was filming with people he didn't necessarily know very well at the time, so he was like, ‘Come on, do this with me. Come do a few videos and see where it goes.’... then it snowballed into where we are now.”

Why Norris and McLaren have committed to each other for the long term

That snowball effect eventually saw Fewtrell become Quadrant's Managing Partner, taking on a bigger role as Norris' focus shifted increasingly towards Formula 1. “As Lando started to fight for the championship... I had to step in,” he explains.

“Because we're close, he can communicate with me, and then I can go into the company. So it made sense for me to step into that role and be that connecting piece between him, me and the brand.”

Fewtrell believes their long friendship has been key to making the partnership work. “We've known each other long enough where we can be very honest. So if we disagree on something, I'll say it straight away, and things get sorted out a bit quicker.

“We can be really clear with communication, so there's no messing around or feeling like we're tiptoeing around the other person.”

Bringing more F1 drivers into the Quadrant world

Norris remains central to Quadrant, but he is increasingly not the only F1 driver appearing within it.

Carlos Sainz, Ollie Bearman, Gabriel Bortoleto and Alex Albon are amongst the familiar faces to have featured in its content as Quadrant looks to reach motorsport fans beyond those who already support its founder.

“We don't necessarily want it to just be that Lando's the only driver we get on,” Fewtrell says.

“I think having the other drivers on has been massive for us to then become a hub of motorsport and build a massive community of people who love racing.

“You don't have to just be a Lando fan to enjoy what we do. I think that's been key, having all the other drivers on so other people can come into Quadrant and get involved in the community because maybe their favourite driver has been on, not just because it's all about Lando.”

The aim is not to recreate the content drivers already produce with their own teams. Instead, Fewtrell says the philosophy is simple: “Let's just enjoy this.” With more than one million YouTube subscribers, Quadrant also gives drivers access to a large audience beyond the traditional race weekend environment.

“For the younger guys that [have] just come onto the grid, it's a benefit for them to come on the channel because we have that audience there already, and it helps them build their own platform,” Fewtrell says.

“So it's good all round, and we also have a nice afternoon!”

From millions of views to meeting fans face to face

As Quadrant's F1 presence has expanded, so has the way it interacts with fans.

The once overwhelmingly digital brand has moved increasingly into physical spaces, with pop-ups in Melbourne and London followed by Quadrant Live at Silverstone’s Made at Vale stage during the 2026 British Grand Prix weekend.

“It was just unbelievable,” Fewtrell says of Made in Vale. “I don't know how to explain it... To see that many people turn up to see yourself, or the brand, is just incredible.

“Sometimes you get lost in the numbers on the screen. You don't realise how many people there actually are. You see videos get 5,000,000 views… but it really puts everything into perspective.”

Those interactions have also shown Fewtrell how communities built around F1 can extend beyond watching what happens on track.

“I've heard so many stories from people that follow us of how they've met friends through Quadrant,” he explains.

“It’s that sense of community, making people feel like they're a part of what we're doing and belonging. It's a place where they can come and enjoy. It's a safe space.

“People come into the pop-up, chat with us, catch up, ask about the last video and get a T-shirt. We're all wearing the same stuff. It's little things like that, which I think actually mean quite a lot.”

Why F1 Arcade is the next step

That focus will continue around the Italian Grand Prix when Quadrant partners with Viagogo to take one of its race watch-alongs offline at the F1 Arcade.

The event includes F1 Arcade's simulators, giveaways and interactive race predictions, plus a pre-race Q&A with Fewtrell and other members of the Quadrant team. The motorsport brand had already experimented with watch-alongs online. Bringing one into a physical F1 space felt like a natural progression.

“We did the watch-alongs online quite a few times, and there's definitely something we can capitalise on doing it in person and having people there,” Fewtrell says.

“Again, there's that community aspect of it. We're really focusing on building that community and doing more stuff in person, face to face as much as we can.

“So I think a watch-along felt like the next step.”

It is an interesting place for Fewtrell to find himself six years after stepping away from racing. He did not reach F1 in the way he imagined as a child, but the sport remains threaded through his work, friendships and a business bringing fans closer to the drivers.

Fewtrell’s hopes for the future

Fewtrell says he is now in a good place with not making it to Formula 1 and does not dwell on it... most of the time.

“Only on the occasional night, it just creeps up on me,” he admits. “You know, you're lying in bed, and something horrible just comes up.”

Nor has he completely closed the door on being a racing driver again. Asked what he would like to achieve next, the answer quickly returns to the cockpit.

“I would love to race in Le Mans at some point for sure, Le Mans or Daytona. I want to get back in the car,” he says. “That's probably a big dream, but I'd love to do that.

“I just want to be happy. That's what it's all about. I used to overthink a lot about many things and stress, so I've really tried to simplify life down, and the main things are all there.

“That's all that matters really.”

title: Lando Norris laments 'useless' McLaren car after 'painful' qualifying
excerpt:
Lando Norris has branded his McLaren "useless" at Monza after a difficult qualifying session consigned him to eighth on the grid for the Italian Grand Prix.

The reigning F1 drivers' champion was actually ninth-fastest at the Temple of Speed, but Kimi Antonelli's power unit penalties will see him move up to the fourth row of the grid.

The MCL40 is struggling with the characteristics of the chassis not suited to the circuit profile of Monza, which is predominantly straights and slow-speed corners.

The car is more aerodynamically draggy than its F1 rivals, and McLaren's gearbox ratios give up roughly 10kph to Mercedes, with the same power unit, in straight-line speed, something that has hindered the Woking-based team this weekend.

That, coupled with the vital need for a good slipstream at Monza, left Norris powerless to salvage another strong qualifying performance after two consecutive pole positions after Oscar Piastri made a mistake at Turn 1 on the final push laps in Q3.

That error from the Australian meant that his team-mate could not be afforded the same benefit he had earlier received, which helped him to third on the grid, behind Pierre Gasly and George Russell.

(Although Piastri has since been handed a three-place grid penalty for impeding Liam Lawson in Q2.)

"I don't think anything didn't work out; it's just that we needed a good slipstream, Norris told media, including RacingNews365, when reflecting on his session and the lock-up from Piastri that ruined his chances of better.

"I had priority in terms of — I had to go out of the pit lane first on Q3 run 1, which meant Oscar had a couple of cars ahead of him, and I just had the one of Antonelli.

"And most of my time loss is just in the straights, so it's nothing I can do. It wasn't my best lap either; I'm not going to deny that, but pretty much the majority of my time is just lost in the straights.

"And, of course, on the second run, it's my time to go behind and get a better slipstream, and that certainly didn't go as I'd hoped.

"So, nothing I can really complain about. We're just unlucky today, and that's the price you pay for being first in a pit lane and having to go out first."

The most 'painful' thing for Norris

However, he rejected the idea that Piastri returning to the track after missing the first chicane cost him any additional time, pointing out that it merely scuppered any possibility of him qualifying higher up the order.

In addition, the 13-time grand prix winner was quick to stress how poorly the MCL40 is suited to the specific requirements of the Temple of Speed.

"It cost me because I had no slipstream; it doesn't matter," Norris added when asked if the sister car going off ahead of him at Turn 1 impeded him.

"We're useless as a car [here]; we're so slow on the straight — we have to have a good slipstream, otherwise we're not quick enough.

"Oscar made use of a good slipstream, and he made it work. My chance never came around, so I just have to take it on the chin."

Norris agreed when asked if it is a perfect storm of factors, across the gear ratios, the drag of the MCL40, its dislike of slow-speed corners and the brake issue he experienced in qualifying.

"Pretty much," he immediately responded, having endured a brake issue from Q1, which left him with little confidence heading into corners.

"I think that the most painful thing this weekend is just a straight-line speed deficit... We needed to be like incredibly close to someone — I had a one-car tow, and I lost two tenths to Oscar, who had a two-car tow. So it's just painful in that sense. But otherwise, it's just what we got to live with for now.

But it's a good example of why I said before that we needed to keep pushing, improving in certain areas, and this was an area we knew we'd not be very strong in."

title: Lewis Hamilton issues Ferrari instruction in hunt of dream home victory
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton has highlighted the importance of Ferrari needing to work as a team as it seeks a home victory on Sunday at the Italian Grand Prix.

Throughout practice, Ferrari appeared to be a threat at the front of the field at Monza.

However, it endured a more challenging outing during qualifying, with Hamilton narrowly avoiding a painful Q2 exit by just 0.001s.

At the end of Q3, the seven-time champion found himself in fifth place, behind team-mate Charles Leclerc.

Hamilton was left to rue a messy end to the session as he outlined that a less-than-ideal position in the queue hindered his rhythm.

“Because everyone was waiting, Charles didn't want to go out first,” Hamilton told media including RacingNews365.

“We had to wait, wait, wait and then only got one push. It made it pretty challenging for us.

“Q3, I didn't have any wheels on the car, and everyone left whilst my engine was running. I went out like 25 seconds behind them all.

“That just put me out of rhythm because when you're following another car, and when you're in that tow, you arrive much faster, so the braking zones are different.

“When you're on your own, when you lose the tow, a lot of time is lost in the tow.”

Hamilton will advance up to fourth place on the starting grid as Oscar Piastri has been handed a three-place grid penalty for impeding Liam Lawson during qualifying.

With no challenger now positioned between the Ferrari duo and Mercedes' Russell, Hamilton asserted Ferrari must play a team game on Sunday to make sure it finishes ahead of the Silver Arrow.

“It's definitely positive to progress [up the grid],” Hamilton added.

“Of course, there's some fighting chance, hopefully, with George. That's one Mercedes up front.

“So hopefully that gives us a chance to work as a team to try and topple them.”

title: Oscar Piastri handed damaging grid penalty for Italian Grand Prix
excerpt:
Oscar Piastri has been handed a three-place grid penalty for the Italian Grand Prix after being found guilty of impeding during qualifying at Monza.

The McLaren driver ended qualifying in third place and was due to start on the second row of the grid, behind Pierre Gasly and George Russell.

However, Piastri was facing an investigation from the stewards, who appeared to hold up Liam Lawson during Q2.

Lawson felt that his lap was significantly hindered as a result and the New Zealander failed to progress into the top 10 shootout.

After the session, Piastri went to see the stewards, who determined that the Australian was at fault.

Detailing their verdict, the stewards said: “On leaving the pits, the driver of Car 81 was advised that “Verstappen, Lawson and Sainz just crossing, Sainz has pitted, Just Verstappen and Lawson, watch out for them as you join”.

“The driver of Car 81 stated that he was not alerted to the fact that VER and LAW were on push laps but realised as he was almost at turn 1 that VER was on a push lap. He slowed significantly and kept to the right to allow VER to pass but was unable to do anything to avoid impeding LAW who was close behind.

“The Stewards accept that with the information he had, and the situation he was placed in, the driver of Car 81 had, at this stage, no other options available and hence, inadvertently, and also unnecessarily, impeded Car 30.

“Therefore the standard penalty of a drop of 3 grid positions is imposed.”

Piastri's penalty means Charles Leclerc, Lewis Hamilton and Max Verstappen will all move up one place each.

title: Max Verstappen calls for Red Bull investigation after car 'failure'
excerpt:
Max Verstappen has called on Red Bull to investigate a peculiar issue that hindered his performance during qualifying at the Italian Grand Prix.

The Dutchman entered the session after enjoying a positive FP3 outing, in which he managed to finish inside the top three.

However, he was unable to remain in the fight at the front for qualifying and slipped to sixth place at the end of Q3.

During the session, he was complaining about an issue with his rear axle and voiced his frustration that the problem occurred at such an important part of the weekend.

“In FP3, we actually had a very good improvement overnight,” he said.

“The car was in a much better window, but we didn't really touch the car too much going into qualifying.

“I suddenly had a feeling that something failed on the rear axle again, not the wing, but something else mechanically, which we have to look into again.

“It's not the first time this happened, but it happened at random times over the weekend.

“Unfortunately, now it happened at the most important part.”

Verstappen was also due to be towed around Q3 by team-mate Liam Lawson - however, the New Zealander failed to advance into the final session after being blocked by Oscar Piastri during Q2.

However, Verstappen insisted it made little difference to his own result due to the problems he was having behind the wheel.

“When you have these kind of problems, it becomes super difficult to drive,” he said.

“The car is not compliant anymore when it should [be] over bumps and kerbs, and that's just costing lap time.

“I actually thought that with how the car was responding in FP3, I didn't think I was fighting for pole, but it was quite a comfortable car to drive for once.

“That was actually really nice but unfortunately we picked up another problem.”

title: George Russell hilariously reveals chess game foreshadowed shock Monza qualifying result
excerpt:
George Russell has shared how he dismissed the idea of Pierre Gasly beating him in qualifying for the Italian Grand Prix during a friendly game of chess just minutes before the start of the grid-setting session at Monza.

The Alpine driver went on to clinch a surprise pole position against all odds at the Temple of Speed, beating the Briton into second by eight hundredths of a second.

It is the first pole of his career, and the first for a French driver since Jean Alesi's for Benetton at the same circuit 29 years ago.

Also the venue of Gasly's sole grand prix victory in 2020, it is Alpine's first pole since the team rebranded from Renault.

"Firstly, massive congrats to Pierre because that's an incredible performance," the Mercedes driver said after qualifying.

"We were actually finishing a game of chess about 15 minutes before qualifying, and he beat me there.

"And I thought, 'Well, I think I'll beat you in qualifying', and here we are: he's ahead of me again.

"So huge congrats to him. Of course, I was disappointed not to get the pole position. It was a bit messy with Verstappen opening the lap; I did the lap very close.

"But Pierre and Alpine have been super fast even from Q1. So happy to see them get a good result."

title: Pierre Gasly charts 'nine-year' chase after spectacular Monza pole upset
excerpt:
Pierre Gasly has recalled his "nine-year" chase for an F1 pole position after securing his first in 191 attempts at the Italian Grand Prix.

Gasly, who topped Q1, took the first pole in F1 history for Alpine, and was the first pole for Team Enstone since Fernando Alonso at the 2009 Hungarian Grand Prix.

At the place where he took his first F1 win in 2020, Gasly's pole was the first for a French driver since Jean Alesi at the 1997 Italian GP.

The time of a 1:21.786 was 0.080s faster than George Russell's, with Gasly, who lost his Monaco podium, becoming the 109th different pole-sitter in F1 history, and the first new one since Kimi Antonelli in China earlier this year.

"It was amazing. It was an incredible qualifying from the first lap in Q1," Gasly explained.

"I felt very good in the car, and was trying to chip a little bit away every single session, and then yeah, at the end, it felt like a very good lap.

"But I'm so happy. It's been nine years trying to chase and get the opportunity to get a pole position, and to win my first race at Monza, and get my first pole position at this track, I think there is something special around here."

title: Liam Lawson set to take Red Bull grid penalty
excerpt:
Liam Lawson is set to incur a grid penalty for the Italian Grand Prix, with Red Bull introducing new power unit components to Isack Hadjar's allocation, RacingNews365 understands.

Despite the Frenchman sitting out at Monza as he continues to recover from the wrist injury he sustained during the F1 summer break, the new parts are assigned to his RB22, not the driver in the cockpit, specifically.

Therefore, Lawson will not face a double-jeopardy-like situation when he returns to his usual Racing Bulls car, which may not be until after the Spanish Grand Prix next week.

On Friday at the Temple of Speed, Red Bull technical director Pierre Waché suggested the New Zealander would take the grid drop, which is why he ran a slightly different run plan during FP2.

The 24-year-old will take a new internal combustion engine (ICE), which is the sixth of four allowed in a season, a sixth turbocharger of the four permitted, and a sixth of four allocated exhaust sets.

Hadjar's Red Bull was already past conformity with the regulations on those three specific components, and the team has opted to go beyond the pool on two more.

As such, there will be a new motor generator unit-kinetic (MGU-K) and power unit ancillary component (PU-ANC) in the back of the RB22, with those at four of three allowed and seven of six permitted, respectively.

Monza is a common venue for teams to take a grid drop due to the vast overtaking opportunities available during the race.

Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli and Williams' Alex Albon have already been fitted with new components and will line up at the back on Sunday.

title: 2026 Italian Grand Prix - F2 Monza Sprint results
excerpt:
Joshua Dürksen roared to victory in the F2 Sprint Race at Monza, beating John Bennett, who started from reverse grid pole position.

Oliver Goethe rounded out the podium places in the Italian Grand Prix support race at the Temple of Speed, with Noel Leon and Nikola Tsolov completing the top five.

Martinius Stenshorne, Alex Dunne and Laurens van Hoepen also scored points, with those covering the top eight finishers.

Dürksen also secured the extra point for posting the fastest lap in the 21-lap race, which was twice interrupted by safety cars.

First, championship contender Rafael Camara, who will start the Feature Race from pole, spun after the first chicane and could not get his Invicta Racing car going again.

Then, later, Roman Bilinski spun his DAMS Lucas Oil machine, hitting the wall and also going into retirement.

title: How young Max Verstappen left karting boss stunned
excerpt:
Max Verstappen's old karting boss has opened up on what the Dutchman was truly like at the start of his career.

Giancarlo Tinini, the Italian owner of karting manufacturer CRG, has offered a rare insight into the early years of Max Verstappen, recalling the moment he first laid eyes on the four-time world champion and immediately recognised something special.

Speaking to De Telegraaf from Monza, where he was attending as a guest of the Verstappen family, Tinini reflected on what set the Red Bull driver apart from an exceptionally young age.

"What stands out most in my mind is Max's enormous drive to race," Tinini said. "He always wanted to push the limits, in every situation.

"Even when he was very young, he was already incredibly professional and completely focused on what he was doing. You could clearly see that he wasn't just there to drive a few laps. He always wanted to understand how he could go even faster."

Verstappen signed a factory contract with CRG in November 2009, with Tinini already having an existing relationship with the family before the deal was formalised.

"I already knew his father and mother, so there was already a connection," he said. "Max has been one of CRG's best ambassadors.

"We're all very proud that he was part of our team and of what we've achieved together."

For Tinini, 2013 stands as the defining chapter of their time together. "That was the year 2013," Tinini added. "Max won two European championships and a world title that year.

"He was fighting for another world championship, in the KF class, but that was derailed after a collision. All in all, though, it was a fantastic season. A wonderful way to wrap things up."

The CRG owner also revealed that, despite his existing ties to the Verstappen family, he had no prior knowledge of Max when he first saw him on track. The impression, however, was instant.

"I can still remember that [the first time] very well," Tinini said. "Max was still too young to officially compete in an international race. I saw a CRG kart on the track with the number 3, without any real stickers, just the name 'Max.'"

"I had no idea who it was, but I was impressed by what he showed. I wanted to find out who he was right away, ran into Jos, and asked if he was one of his drivers.

"Jos said, 'Well, no, this is my son.' Max was still very young, but I immediately asked if they were interested in joining our team. It was pretty clear right away just how talented he was."

title: George Russell throws down Ferrari Monza pole challenge as Lewis Hamilton nearest rival
excerpt:
It is George Russell who emerged fastest from the final practice session from the Italian Grand Prix at Monza.

George Russell is the favourite for Italian Grand Prix pole position, with Lewis Hamilton emerging as his closest rival in Free Practice 3.

In the final 60 minutes at Monza, Russell clocked a 1:22.219 to top his second session of the weekend, after FP2, with Hamilton's Ferrari slotting in 0.226s behind.

Max Verstappen rounded out the top three in an otherwise tight session as just over two-tenths seperated Hamilton in second and Arvid Lindblad in seventh.

Qualifying starts later this afternoon at 15:00 local time, 14:00 BST.

With drivers keen to find the precious tow and slipstream to aid lap times, most of the action was centred around the second half of the session, with Kimi Antonelli topping the initial times, although he will carry a 30-place grid penalty for an engine change.

Russell ultimately topped the times on a 1:22.219, being aided by the tow from Antonelli through Curva Grande and into Turn 4, with Hamilton getting the tow from the McLaren of Oscar Piastri.

Hamilton slotted in behind Russell on his second attempt at a soft-tyre run having aborted his first attempt having gone purple through sector one.

Verstappen was third on a 1:22.569, with Antonelli 0.011s behind in the sister Mercedes.

Lando Norris was fifth for McLaren ahead of Charles Leclerc, Lindblad, Piastri, Pierre Gasly, and Franco Colapinto, who rounded out the top 10.

Verstappen was noted by the stewards for an incident with Hamilton at the end of the session, where he divebombed into Turn 1 after feeling Hamilton had aggrieved him at Parabolica.

The Williams drivers Carlos Sainz and Alex Albon will be investigated for yellow flag infringements, whilst Russell escaped sanction for an alleged impeding on Piastri at Lesmo 1.

title: 2026 F1 Italian Grand Prix - Monza Free Practice 3 results
excerpt:
George Russell continued his fine form at the Italian Grand Prix, comfortably topping the final free practice session at Monza, over two-tenths clear of Lewis Hamilton.

Max Verstappen rounded out the top three, whilst Kimi Antonelli and Lando Norris completed the top five at the Temple of Speed.

Despite Russell's electric pace giving him a seemingly comfortable buffer heading into qualifying, where his penalty-bound team-mate will be aiding his efforts, the fight for second place is close, with only three more tenths down to eighth.

It was another relatively quiet session, with Liam Lawson spinning at the first chicane one of the standout moments from the third hour of practice running.

Oscar Piastri was particularly grumpy, taking to team radio on multiple occasions to vent his frustration at traffic and the difficulties he encountered getting an adequate tow for his qualifying simulations. The McLaren driver ended up eighth, after Russell ruined his penultimate effort.

Verstappen and Hamilton proved that there is no love lost between them in the dying moments. After the Ferrari driver cheekily snuck by into the final corner before their last push laps, the Dutchman dive-bombed him into Turn 1, scuppering both their attempts. The two drivers were noted by the stewards for the episode but not further action was taken.

Both Williams drivers are under investigation for potential yellow flag infringements, after Alex Albon was also handed a warning for incorrectly using an escape road.
